lastCommit.message:
[ota-hal] OTA-1658: the pouch actually heals

Owner, playing OTA-1657: "the heals load into the pouch and it can collapse, I
can open heals in battle, but when tapped they don't do anything."

He is right. This is a fix for a defect I shipped four hours ago, and the cause
is the argument I made for it in OTA-1657's own commit message.

⚠⚠⚠ I ROUTED THE TAP THROUGH `useInventoryItem` AND CALLED THAT CORRECTNESS.
The message said: "not 'like', the SAME action the pack's USE button fires — so
the heal, the stamina, the cure, the stack decrement and every downstream hook
stay one implementation." Every word of that is true. What I never did was check
what that action does in the one place this button was built for:

    useInventoryItem  →  submitPlayerAction(`use ${name}`)
    submitPlayerAction, first line:
        if (!trimmed || get().pendingRolls) return;

⚠ COMBAT IN THIS GAME *IS* `pendingRolls`. Every swing sets it and it stays set
while the dice are on screen. So in a fight the tap reached a guard clause and
returned — no heal, no refusal, no log line. That is the worst failure a button
can have, because it is indistinguishable from a dead control: he tapped, nothing
happened, and the game gave him no reason.

⚠⚠ THE LESSON WAS ALREADY WRITTEN DOWN, FORTY LINES FROM THE CODE I ADDED.
`dropInventoryItem`, in the same file, carries a comment about threading a UI
action through `submitPlayerAction`, watching it work in a probe, watching it
fail on a real id, and concluding the BODY has to be callable directly — "an
identifier whose resolution depends on whether it happens to look like a word is
not a mechanism, it is a coincidence." I added a new UI action a few dozen lines
away and made the same class of mistake anyway.

THE FIX is the path the combat bar already used: `useHealBatch`, a direct store
action. HP, stamina AND the OTA-1573 cures, one off the stack, logged, persisted
— with no parser and no roll gate between the tap and the heal. The OTA-1657 GOAL
was right (one implementation, not two); the ROUTE was wrong.

⚠ THE SUITE REPRODUCES THE DEFECT BEFORE IT PROVES THE FIX. ota1658 boots a real
store, damages the player, puts a roll on the screen — which is what combat is —
and asserts that the OLD call changes the player's HP by exactly nothing. Then it
asserts the new call heals through that same state, spends exactly one from the
stack, leaves the pocket loaded, empties cleanly on the last one, and still works
with no roll pending. A fix whose test cannot fail against the old code is not a
regression test, it is a description.

⚠ AND THE RULE IT LEAVES, pinned: a button that must work mid-fight calls a store
action DIRECTLY. The bandolier throw already did (`throwFromBandolier`); the heals
popup now does too, and the suite asserts both so a third rack gets it right by
default.

One honest note on the log assertion: `appendLog` does not land synchronously in
the jest harness — measured, the heal applies and the in-process feed stays empty
— so asserting through `gameLog` would test the harness, not the game. That one
claim is pinned at the source instead, on the same `world` line the inventory
heal emits.

⚠ AND OTA-1657'S OWN SUITE WENT RED, CORRECTLY: it pinned
`useInventoryItem(it.name)` — so it was pinning the BUG, and went green over a
button that did nothing in a fight. That is the sharpest lesson here: a source
pin certifies the code you wrote, never the behaviour you promised. Repointed to
the working route, with the history written beside it.

Gates: all 18 green by exit code. Full suite green — 1121 suites, 11,612 tests.
